subject: Auditing and Ethics
question_html: As per the U.N. Handbook on Government Auditing in Developing Countries, government auditing is best described as:

options.A: The objective, systematic, professional and independent examination of financial, administrative and other operations of a public entity, made subsequently to their execution, for evaluating and verifying them and presenting a report with conclusions and recommendations
options.B: A subjective, informal review conducted only at the discretion of the audited department, with no independent standing
options.C: An examination confined exclusively to the financial statements of government companies, excluding all other public entities
options.D: A review conducted only before the expenditure is incurred, and never subsequent to its execution

answer_html:
A. The objective, systematic, professional and independent examination of financial, administrative and other operations of a public entity, made subsequently to their execution, for evaluating and verifying them and presenting a report with conclusions and recommendations

The U.N. Handbook defines government auditing as the objective, systematic, professional and independent examination of financial, administrative and other operations of a public entity, made subsequently to their execution, for evaluating/verifying them and presenting a report with conclusions and recommendations, and, for financial statements, expressing a professional opinion on fairness of presentation.

question_html: Regarding the appointment and removal of the Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG) of India, which of the following is correct?

options.A: The C&AG is appointed by the Parliament directly through a floor vote, and may be removed by a simple majority of either House
options.B: The C&AG is appointed by the Prime Minister and may be removed at the Prime Minister's discretion at any time
options.C: The C&AG is appointed by the President of India and shall not be removed from office except on the ground of proven mis-behaviour or incapacity, in the same manner as a Judge of the Supreme Court
options.D: The C&AG is appointed by the Chief Justice of India and may be removed only by the Supreme Court

answer_html:
C. The C&AG is appointed by the President of India and shall not be removed from office except on the ground of proven mis-behaviour or incapacity, in the same manner as a Judge of the Supreme Court

The Constitution guarantees the C&AG's independence by providing for appointment by the President and removal only on the ground of proven mis-behaviour or incapacity, following the same procedure as removal of a Supreme Court Judge (a majority of not less than 2/3rd of members present and voting in each House).

question_html: For the purpose of the C&AG's duty to audit the receipts and expenditure of a body or authority substantially financed by grants or loans from the Consolidated Fund, a body or authority is deemed to be 'substantially financed' when:

options.A: The grant or loan in a financial year is not less than Rs. 1 crore, regardless of what percentage of total expenditure it represents
options.B: The grant or loan constitutes any percentage of total expenditure, however small, provided some amount has been received from the Consolidated Fund
options.C: The grant or loan in a financial year is not less than Rs. 25 lakhs and constitutes not less than 75% of the total expenditure of that body or authority
options.D: The body or authority is wholly owned by the Central Government, with no reference to any grant or loan amount

answer_html:
C. The grant or loan in a financial year is not less than Rs. 25 lakhs and constitutes not less than 75% of the total expenditure of that body or authority

A body or authority is deemed 'substantially financed' for this purpose where the grant or loan from the Consolidated Fund in a financial year is not less than Rs. 25 lakhs and not less than 75% of the total expenditure of that body or authority.

options.B: Public authorities are free to exercise their powers of sanctioning expenditure to their own direct or indirect advantage, provided it is disclosed

question_html: The audit of government receipts provides for checking, among other matters:

question_html: Regarding donations and grants received by an NGO, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Corpus contributions are always shown as income in the Income and Expenditure Account of the NGO, never as a liability
options.B: A Revolving Fund contribution is meant to be spent once and permanently, with no expectation of recovery or re-lending
options.C: Contributions towards the corpus and towards a Revolving Fund are treated identically in every respect, with no distinction drawn by the chapter
options.D: A contribution made towards the capital or corpus of an NGO is known as a corpus contribution and is shown as a liability in the balance sheet, whereas the objective of a contribution towards a Revolving Fund is to rotate the amount by giving temporary loans to beneficiaries and recovering them for re-lending

subject: Auditing and Ethics
question_html: Which of the following is cited as an advantage of audit of a partnership firm?

options.A: Audited accounts eliminate entirely the need for the partnership to maintain any books of account going forward
options.B: Audited accounts constitute reliable evidence for computing amounts due to a retiring partner or the representative of a deceased partner in respect of their share of capital, profits and goodwill, on dissolution
options.C: Audited accounts automatically extend the duration of the partnership without any need for renewal of the partnership agreement
options.D: Audited accounts exempt the partnership from any further scrutiny by banks when applying for future loans

answer_html:
B. Audited accounts constitute reliable evidence for computing amounts due to a retiring partner or the representative of a deceased partner in respect of their share of capital, profits and goodwill, on dissolution

Advantages of audit of a partnership firm include: settling disputes among partners; providing reliable evidence on dissolution/retirement/death of a partner for computing amounts due; reliability for banks and prospective purchasers; assistance in admission of a new partner; and control as a safeguard against undue advantage by a working partner.

question_html: A Limited Liability Partnership (LLP), governed by the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, is best described as:

options.A: A form of business organisation that can be formed by a single individual, with no requirement for any partner or designated partner
options.B: A form of business organisation that must always have at least 7 partners, in the same manner as a public company requires a minimum number of members
options.C: A form of business organisation that is governed exclusively by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, with no separate governing statute
options.D: A form of business organisation which enshrines in itself the advantages of both the Company and Partnership forms of organisation, requiring a minimum of 2 partners, at least 2 of whom must be Designated Partners holding a Designated Partner Identification Number (DPIN)

question_html: As per Rule 24 of the LLP Rules, 2009, an LLP is required to get its accounts audited unless:

options.A: Its turnover does not exceed Rs. 40 lakh in any financial year, and its contribution does not exceed Rs. 25 lakh
options.B: Its turnover does not exceed Rs. 1 crore in any financial year, regardless of its contribution amount

question_html: Regarding the appointment of an auditor of an LLP, which of the following is correct?

options.A: The auditor of an LLP must always be appointed by the Registrar of Companies directly, with no role for the designated partners or partners

options.D: The designated partners have no power to appoint an auditor to fill a casual vacancy; only the partners collectively may do so

options.B: Ignore entirely any subscriptions or donations received through online/digital payment modes, confining the audit to cash receipts only

question_html: As per AS 19, which of the following is one of the attributes that would qualify a lease arrangement as a Finance Lease?

options.A: The lease arrangement is treated purely as a renting arrangement, with lease payments recorded solely as operating expenses
options.B: The lease term is for the major part of the economic life of the asset, even if title is not transferred, or the present value of minimum lease payments at inception amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of the leased asset
options.C: The lessee has no option whatsoever to purchase the asset at any point during or after the lease term
options.D: The leased assets are of a generic, non-specialised nature that could readily be used by any other party without modification

answer_html:
B. The lease term is for the major part of the economic life of the asset, even if title is not transferred, or the present value of minimum lease payments at inception amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of the leased asset

Under AS 19, a Finance Lease is characterised by attributes such as: transfer of ownership at the end of the lease term; a bargain purchase option reasonably certain to be exercised; the lease term covering the major part of the asset's economic life; the present value of minimum lease payments amounting to substantially all of the asset's fair value at inception; or the leased asset being of such a specialised nature that only the lessee can use it without major modification.

subject: Auditing and Ethics
question_html: Regarding the distinction between a Finance Lease and an Operating Lease, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Under an operating lease, the asset always appears on the lessee's balance sheet, exactly as it would under a finance lease
options.B: Under a finance lease, the lessee can never claim depreciation, since ownership always remains with the lessor throughout and after the lease term
options.C: There is no accounting or tax difference whatsoever between a finance lease and an operating lease; the distinction is purely one of terminology
options.D: Under a finance lease, the lease payments are treated like a loan arrangement, so the asset appears on the lessee's balance sheet and the lessee can claim both interest and depreciation, whereas under an operating lease, lease payments are treated as expenses (as in a renting arrangement) and the asset does not appear on the lessee's balance sheet, with no depreciation claimable by the lessee

answer_html:
D. Under a finance lease, the lease payments are treated like a loan arrangement, so the asset appears on the lessee's balance sheet and the lessee can claim both interest and depreciation, whereas under an operating lease, lease payments are treated as expenses (as in a renting arrangement) and the asset does not appear on the lessee's balance sheet, with no depreciation claimable by the lessee

A finance lease is accounted for like a loan (asset on the lessee's balance sheet, with interest and depreciation both claimable by the lessee), while an operating lease is accounted for like renting (lease payments as expense, no asset recognition or depreciation for the lessee) - reflecting the underlying transfer, or non-transfer, of substantially all risks and rewards of ownership.

question_html: Which type of audit is most relevant to the observation that no assessment has been made of whether the rural pipeline project achieved its intended improvement in access to potable water?

options.B: Audit of sanctions, since this is concerned only with whether expenditure was covered by a competent sanction, not with outcomes
options.C: Performance audit, since it is an appraisal of the performance of programmes, schemes or projects with reference to the overall targeted objectives, as well as the efficiency of the means adopted for attaining them
options.D: Audit against rules and orders, since this is concerned only with conformity to financial rules, not with outcomes

answer_html:

Performance audit (covering efficiency, economy and effectiveness) appraises whether programmes, schemes and projects involving large financial expenditure are being run economically and yielding the results expected of them - directly relevant to assessing whether the pipeline project achieved its intended objective.
